authoritativeText.text:
35. Measuring the speeds of gas molecules

Equation $(3-15)$ can be used to calculate a statistical measure of molecular speed for a classical ideal gas in thermal equilibrium.
The ideal-gas model treats molecules as particles whose own size and interactions between collisions can be neglected.

Here, classical means using the ordinary motion-energy model rather than quantum effects.
Thermal equilibrium means a settled thermal state whose average behavior is not changing with time.

Substituting $\overline E=\frac{m\overline{v^2}}{2}$ gives the average of the squared speeds, called the mean square speed.
The mass in this expression is the mass of one molecule.

Measure speeds from a viewpoint moving with the gas as a whole, so its overall flow is not counted.
Use absolute temperature in kelvins: this scale is measured from absolute zero, not from the zero on the Celsius scale.

$\overline{v^2}=\frac{3kT}{m}.$
$(3-17)$

Since $k=\frac{R}{N_A}$ and $\mu=mN_A$, formula $(3-17)$ can be written as $\overline{v^2}=\frac{3RT}{\mu}$.
Taking the square root of the average squared speed gives the **root mean square speed**.
This means: square the speeds, take their average, then take its square root.

Below, the bar over the speed symbol follows the textbook's notation for this root mean square speed.
It does not mean adding the speeds and dividing by the number of molecules.
It is also not the average of velocity vectors, which include direction:

$\overline v=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{\mu}}=\sqrt{\frac{3kT}{m}}.$
$(3-18)$

Formula $(3-18)$ gives the root mean square speed of nitrogen molecules at $t=0^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
Using the textbook's precision, this is $\overline v=500$ m/s, since $\mu=0.028$ kg/mol.
At the same temperature, hydrogen molecules have a root mean square speed of $\overline v=1800$ m/s.

The calculation must use the corresponding absolute temperature, not the Celsius number directly.
These values describe a group of molecules;
not every nitrogen or hydrogen molecule moves at that speed.

The textbook describes how the calculated molecular speeds surprised some physicists in the second half of the nineteenth century.
It compares them with artillery-shell speeds, explaining why this led to questions about kinetic theory.
Its contrasting example is a smell taking roughly a few tens of seconds to travel from one corner of a room to another.

That time is the textbook's estimate for its example, not a fixed time for every room.
The speed of molecular thermal motion is not the speed at which a smell spreads across a room.
Air currents also affect the spreading.

In the collision model for a dilute gas, molecules repeatedly change direction, so a path can be drawn as a complicated zigzag (Figure $51$).
A molecule can travel quickly between collisions, but the different directions mean its total distance traveled is not its net displacement.
Even after a few minutes, its typical net displacement can be much smaller than its total path length.

This does not mean that each molecule moves slowly in one direction.
For a molecule traveling from point $A$ to point $B$, the zigzag path is usually much longer than the straight-line distance $AB$.



Figure 51

Molecular-beam speed measurements provide an experimental test of the kinetic theory behind formula $(3-18)$.
The textbook describes an experiment performed by Stern in 1920.

A speed distribution describes how many atoms have the different speeds.
The instrument records only atoms that pass through its slit and collect on the wall.

This selected sample and the way it is recorded need interpretation before comparison with the gas's root mean square speed.
Not every measured average is the root mean square speed.

The apparatus has two concentric cylinders, $A$ and $B$, rigidly connected so that they rotate together (Figure $52$).
Concentric here means that one cylinder is nested inside the other around the same central line.

That line is their axis.
A thin platinum wire $C$, coated with silver, lies along the inner cylinder's axis.
An electric current heats the wire, and a narrow slit $O$ is cut in the inner cylinder's wall.

Air is pumped out to reduce collisions between flying atoms and remaining gas.
The outer cylinder $B$ stays at room temperature so that silver atoms can deposit on its inner wall.



Figure 52

First keep the apparatus stationary and heat the wire electrically to evaporate silver, producing silver atoms.
Some atoms pass through slit $O$ and deposit on cylinder $B$'s inner wall.

They form a narrow silver band $D$ opposite the slit (Figure $52$, b).
Next rotate the cylinders at angular speed $\omega$.
Angular speed describes how quickly the apparatus turns.

In the textbook's approximation, atoms fly radially in straight lines at constant speed.
Radially means outward from the common center.
Each radius is the distance from that center to the corresponding cylinder wall, not a diameter.

The time to travel the difference in the cylinder radii, $R_B-R_A$, is $t$.
This flight time starts when the atom passes through the inner cylinder's slit, not when it leaves the wire.

During this time, the cylinder turns through angle $\varphi$.
The atom is approximately collision-free while the outer cylinder keeps turning.

The deposit is therefore shifted from the endpoint of the radius corresponding to slit $O$.
The shift along the outer cylinder's inner wall is an arc length $s$ (Figure $53$).

An arc length is a curved distance along the wall.
In the figure, D marks the wall point currently aligned with the rotating slit, and D-prime marks the atom's impact point.

Here, $s$ is the separation of those wall points caused by rotation, not the atom's straight flight-path length.
Under the textbook's model:
$s=\omega R_Bt.$
$(3-19)$



Figure 53a: the cylinders' position when an atom passes through the slit.
b: their position after time $t$, when that atom reaches the outer cylinder.

In the radial-flight approximation above, the atom's speed from the inner slit to the outer cylinder is $v=\frac{R_B-R_A}{t}.$

Use equation $(3-19)$ to express $t$, then substitute it into the speed formula:
$v=\frac{\omega R_B(R_B-R_A)}{s}.$

If $\omega$, $R_A$, and $R_B$ are known, measuring the rotation-induced band shift $S$ lets us estimate the silver atoms' flight speed under this model.
The capital letter here follows the textbook and denotes the same wall shift as the lowercase letter in the preceding formula.

Atoms with different speeds have different flight times and shifts.
The silver band consists only of atoms that passed through the slit and were collected on the wall.

It is not automatically a representative average of every atom in the gas.
Its position and width need interpretation using how many atoms have each speed and how the instrument records them.

The textbook describes agreement with theory as support for formulas $(3-18)$ and $(3-15)$.
This does not make one arbitrary band position, or an arithmetic average speed, equal to the root mean square speed.

Equation $(3-18)$ also expresses a temperature-and-mass relation useful for discussing the thermal kinetic energy of Brownian particles.
A Brownian particle is a tiny particle suspended in a liquid, moving irregularly as the surrounding molecules push it unevenly.

Consider it in classical thermal equilibrium with that liquid.
Its kinetic energy here means the energy of movement through space, not rotation.

The equipartition model assigns equal average motion energy to each independent spatial direction.
This is an average, not equal energy in every direction at every moment.
Under these conditions, its average kinetic energy is described by formula $(3-15)$.

The corresponding estimate of root mean square speed is:
$\overline v=\sqrt{\frac{3kT}{M}}$.

Here, $M$ is the Brownian particle's mass①.
The bar still means root mean square speed.
Keeping the other conditions fixed, this speed scale increases with temperature and decreases with mass.

The textbook uses this to explain why heavier particles' thermal motion can be hard to notice.
The estimate is not the speed obtained directly from a displacement seen over a finite time under a microscope.

Observed Brownian displacement also depends on liquid resistance, particle size, and observation time.
Mass alone does not determine whether motion exists or can be observed.

① The textbook points out that Brownian motion is very irregular.
Instantaneous velocity means velocity at one moment, whereas an observation interval lasts for some time.

An observed zigzag path should not be treated as a directly measured instantaneous velocity.
Displacement over a finite time can give an average motion on that time scale, but not the thermal-equilibrium root mean square speed above.

Inertia is a finite-mass particle's resistance to a change of motion.
The ideal Brownian diffusion model neglects this effect and describes the spreading of irregular displacements.

In that model, a path has no ordinary instantaneous velocity.
Real particles have finite mass, and a more complete account of their dynamics is needed on sufficiently short time scales when inertia matters.
Thus, "cannot be measured" is not an absolute restriction on every experiment or every time scale.

inventory.description: Two top-view panels, source a/b: apparatus identification at left, static deposition at right. Left: outer cylinder B, inner cylinder A and central axial wire C share a center. O is the slit on the upper-right inner wall. Left: the outer contour also has an unlabelled upper-right break. Preserve that visible break without identifying it as the inner slit or inventing hidden hardware. Left: two solid radius arrows run from C toward the left inner rim and lower-left outer rim; their labels are R_A and R_B. Labels A, B, C, O all retained. Right: two concentric rims and a central black point, two solid radial beam-boundary lines, and a narrow dark deposition band D on the upper-right outer wall. No rotation arrow, dashed guide, numeric radius, calibrated angle, extra panel or scale. The unmeasured inner-to-outer radius ratio is about 0.27. Modern additions: English a/b and uppercase radius labels in ASCII subscript notation R_A and R_B; no lowercase or Greek subscript substitution. Small clean inner slit gaps clarify the slit explicitly located in the authoritative text; no additional opening, apparatus, or measurement is asserted. Circular rims, narrow beam spread and label positions are regularized unmeasured layout, not physical data. Uncertainties: The unlabelled upper-right break in the source outer rim has no separately identified physical role. The source inner slit ink is rough; its semantic location is supported by the frozen text, not inferred as a new component.
